L01:
FlagShip raised a $4.2M seed round, led by Basis Ventures.

It took 18 months to get here. Six of us, building a feature-flag platform on one belief: shipping software shouldn't be scary, and flags belong in the foundation of how teams deliver, not bolted on as an afterthought.

The money goes to three places. Growing the engineering team. Shipping faster for the early customers who bet on us. And making feature management effortless for every developer, which is the part we'll be chasing for years.

To our customers: thank you for trusting us early. To the team: none of this happens without you.

We're hiring. If you want to build developer tools with a team that's still six people, my DMs are open.
L02:
Nine months, 3 teams, and our fintech's monolith is now microservices. Our p99 latency is down 40%.

The technical work turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was alignment: getting 3 teams to agree on service boundaries, ownership, and standards took more energy than any line of code we wrote.

What I'd tell anyone starting a migration like this: begin with the domain, not the technology. Migrate incrementally, because big bangs fail. And celebrate the small wins, because nine months is a long time to wait for one big one.

Deployments that used to take hours now take minutes. Three teams ship independently without stepping on each other.

And to everyone who says microservices are overhyped: sometimes they're exactly the right tool for the job.
L03:
We just opened our first design role.

Founding Designer at our AI startup in Austin. You report to the CEO, you define the visual identity and the design culture from scratch, and you shape how people interact with AI, which I'd argue is one of the most interesting design problems going. Equity is 0.5 to 1%, because the first design hire should own a real piece of what they build.

There's no design system to inherit and nobody to hand you requirements. If you need mature process to do your best work, this role will frustrate you. If you want to be the one who sets the process, there isn't a better seat.

Austin preferred. We'll flex for the right person.

If that's you, or you know exactly who it is, my DMs are open.
L04:
In January I was laid off from a big tech company. Six months later, I'm leading product at a 30-person startup.

The months in between were the hardest of my career. More than 200 applications. Interviews that went nowhere. Long stretches of silence, and days I questioned everything I thought I knew about my own value.

A few things turned out to be true. My job was not my identity, although it took losing one to actually believe that. And the right opportunity was worth the wait, which is easy to type now and was very hard to believe in the middle of it.

To the hiring managers who sent thoughtful rejections instead of silence: it mattered more than you know.

If you're in the middle of a layoff right now, the process is brutal and the silence is worse. You are not your job title. My DMs are open.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same 3 foundation models.

Every week another "revolutionary" agent launches, and every week the pattern repeats: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing the heavy lifting underneath. Prompts are not a moat. Anyone can copy one in an afternoon.

What actually creates defensibility is duller. Workflow depth: being embedded so deep in how a team works that switching hurts. And proprietary data: feedback loops that make the product smarter every day it runs.

The winners won't be the teams with the best demo. They'll be the ones who understand their customers' workflows better than anyone else on the planet.

If you're building an agent startup, one question is worth sitting with: if the model providers shipped your feature tomorrow, what would be left?
L06:
A few days at SaaStr Annual, 40+ conversations with founders, and three things I keep turning over.

PLG has grown up. Product-led stopped being a buzzword; companies are getting sophisticated about layering sales on top of self-serve motions.

AI pricing is unsettled. Seat-based, usage-based, outcome-based: every founder I asked is experimenting, and not one of them sounded confident. Nobody has cracked it.

And community-led growth is back after a few quiet years, except this time people are attaching real ROI expectations to it.

The pricing gap is the thing I keep coming back to. The energy in SaaS right now is unlike anything I've seen in years, and nobody agrees on how to charge for the newest part of it.

If you were there, what stuck with you?
L07:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production.

The models have been ready for a while. Something else is failing.

Two things kill pilots. Data readiness: most enterprises sit on fragmented, inconsistent, poorly governed data, and you can't build production AI on spreadsheets and silos. And process redesign, or the absence of it. Companies bolt AI onto existing workflows and expect magic, when what AI actually demands is that you rethink the workflow. Skip that step and the pilot dies in the demo phase.

The companies getting AI into production did the unglamorous work first: cleaned their data, redesigned their processes, prepared their people for the change.

The technology isn't the bottleneck. We are.
L08:
Clearlens v2 is live.

The two features in it are the two that came up most across 300+ customer interviews this past year. Session replay, so you can watch exactly how users experience your product, moment by moment. And funnel comparison, which puts two conversion funnels side by side so the argument about which flow converts better ends with data.

Fourteen beta customers spent the past few months testing these and telling us exactly where they fell short. Their feedback shaped every screen we shipped.

The thing this release taught me: customers already know what your roadmap should be. You just have to ask, then sit through 300 interviews' worth of answers.

Link's in the first comment.
L09:
The most useful thing I did in ten years of B2B sales took 90 seconds and no talking.

A deal was falling apart on a call. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct said jump in with answers. Instead I shut up. Ninety full seconds of silence, which on a sales call feels excruciating.

In that silence, the prospect talked themselves through their own objection and surfaced the real blocker, one I'd never have guessed. We closed two weeks later.

Ten years in, I think listening is the number one skill in sales. Not pitching, not negotiating, not objection handling. Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them if you let them finish a thought. Sometimes the best discovery question is no question at all.

Talk less. Sell more.
L10:
I'm shutting down Cartful.

Three years, $1.1M raised, 4,000 users, and never the thing that mattered: repeatable revenue.

We celebrated signups while dodging the harder question of who would pay, and why. Users are not customers, and we blurred the two for too long.

One-off deals felt like traction. They weren't. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one. I couldn't.

And we treated runway as something to stretch rather than something to spend. We kept the company alive when we should have been buying answers faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you, and I'm sorry we couldn't get there.
L11:
A few months ago I stopped daily standups for my team of 14.

We replaced them with async written updates. Each morning, everyone posts three things: what they did, what they're doing, what's blocking them. That's the whole system.

Six hours of meetings gone every week. Shipping speed: unchanged. Engineers report fewer interruptions and more deep work.

The awkward conclusion: most standups aren't for the team. They're for the manager. A status ritual dressed up as collaboration.

Written updates also turned out better on their own merits. People think before they write. Updates are searchable months later. Time zones stopped mattering.

Standups aren't always wrong. But if yours feels like a status meeting, it probably is one, and your team already knows it.

Would your team survive the switch?
L12:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam.

Eleven weeks of studying wrapped around a full-time job, and one of the hardest certifications I've attempted.

What actually worked: practice exams. I took 5, and every single one exposed gaps I didn't know I had. Consistency mattered more than intensity, since an hour every day did more for me than eight hours on a Saturday ever managed. Hands-on labs made concepts stick where videos never could. And study time went on my calendar like a meeting. Because it is one.

If you're grinding through a certification around a full-time job right now: it's hard, and it's absolutely possible.

Next up, putting it to work.
L13:
A year ago I became an engineering manager.

The hardest change had nothing to do with meetings or difficult conversations. It was learning to measure my output by my team's work instead of my own commits.

For years, my sense of a day well spent came from shipping: green squares, merged PRs, something concrete to point at by evening. Then my output went invisible. A good week now means all 7 of my direct reports are unblocked and shipping while my own contributions show up exactly nowhere. I felt like an impostor for months.

What year one taught me: most problems are communication problems in disguise. Clarity is the most valuable thing a manager hands out. And the urge to jump in and fix it yourself is precisely the urge to resist.

If you're a new EM wrestling with the same identity shift, you're in good company. It does fade.
L14:
Our on-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter, and the only thing we changed was writing things down.

Documentation has no glamour. Nobody gets promoted for runbooks, and our team of 9 SREs had treated them accordingly. Then we committed. Every incident got a runbook entry, no exceptions. Every repeated page triggered a documentation review. We deleted stale docs as aggressively as we wrote new ones, and runbook quality went into our definition of done.

The systems didn't get better. The knowledge just stopped living exclusively in people's heads.

The ROI of documentation stays invisible until you measure it. Fewer 2 AM wake-ups. Faster onboarding. A calmer rotation, and less bus factor.

If your team is drowning in pages, write a runbook before you evaluate another tool.
L15:
After 3 years fully remote, our company went hybrid: 2 days a week in the office. The scoreboard since then refuses to pick a side.

Retention improved, and our numbers are better than they've been in two years. Onboarding got noticeably faster. Cross-team collaboration feels easier.

And 2 senior people quit over the change, losses that still sting. Trust took a hit during the transition. Some days the office sits half empty and people openly wonder why they commuted.

My conclusion after living through it: there's no right answer to remote vs hybrid. Every model has tradeoffs, every policy disappoints someone, and the only variable you fully control is honesty. We told the team exactly why we made the change and accepted that some people would make a different choice for their lives. I respect that.

Anyone who claims remote vs hybrid is a solved problem is selling something.
L16:
AI won't replace junior developers. It's already changing what junior means, though.

We recently hired 2 junior engineers. Both use AI pair-programming tools daily, and both ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago. By a wide margin. What's shifted is where their value sits: less memorizing syntax and cranking out boilerplate, more reviewing code critically, asking better questions, and understanding the system they're touching.

Today's junior isn't someone who writes simple code slowly. It's someone who orchestrates AI tools, verifies the output, and learns architecture from day one.

Three consequences. Hiring rubrics built around syntax trivia are obsolete. Mentorship matters more, because judgment can't be autocompleted. And the ladder from junior to senior is compressing.

Companies that stop hiring juniors "because AI" are quietly deleting their own senior pipeline.
L17:
Last week a churned customer came back. On their own.

When they left, they'd told us the truth: our seat-based pricing punished them for growing their team. They were paying for licenses nobody used.

So we made the jump to usage-based pricing. It was scary. We modeled the downside a dozen times, and some advisors told us flatly not to do it.

Since the switch: expansion revenue up 22%, sales conversations that start with value instead of license counts, and churned customers returning without a campaign to win them back.

The lesson I keep turning over is that pricing is a statement about whose side you're on. Seat-based rewarded us when customers overbought. Usage-based pays us only when our customers succeed. Lining those up is good ethics that also happens to be good business.

Which is, I suspect, why they came back.
L18:
Six months ago, a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them. This week they signed an offer: frontend developer at an insurance company.

The hard work was entirely theirs. What we did together was mostly unglamorous: weekly check-ins even when progress felt slow, code reviews on real projects instead of toy exercises, 4 mock interviews that got harder each round, and honest conversations about rejection.

The thing that surprised me is what mentorship turned out to require. Not answers. Consistency, especially in the weeks when someone's confidence is wavering.

The industry loves debating whether bootcamp grads can make it. Watching this one do it settled the question for me: with grit and the right support, absolutely.

If you've been writing software for a while, mentor someone. One hour a week can change a career.

And to my mentee, if you're reading this: congratulations. You earned every bit of it.
L19:
We changed one email subject line and open rates jumped 31%.

For months, every email to our 18k subscribers led with the feature: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Solid open rates, nothing special. Then we ran a simple experiment and described the outcome instead. Same email, same list, same send time.

Feature version: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard."
Outcome version: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking."

The first talks about you. The second talks about the reader, and the reader opened it 31% more often.

The lesson is older than email itself, and apparently we still needed the reminder: people open for what a feature does for them. We've since rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails on the same principle, and the gains have held.

Worth auditing your last 10 subject lines. Count how many talk about you.
L20:
Our 12-person team runs the whole company on 5 tools.

Linear holds every task, bug, and project. If it's not in Linear, it doesn't exist. Notion is the company brain: docs, wikis, meeting notes, onboarding. Slack covers communication, with strict channel hygiene to keep the noise down. Figma is where product ideas get real before anyone writes code. And Otto, our homegrown deploy bot: one command and a PR goes to production. Everyone's favorite teammate.

That's the entire stack. Nobody wonders which doc is the source of truth, and nobody pays for overlapping subscriptions.

The principle underneath: every new tool adds a tax. Context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations. A tool gets added only when the pain of not having it beats that tax, and most candidates never clear the bar.

Simplicity is a competitive advantage.
L21:
I just took my first real break in 4 years. Two weeks: no Slack, no email, no quick calls.

The first days were uncomfortable. I checked my phone out of habit, felt guilty, and half believed things would fall apart without me. They didn't.

The useful part came after. I got back, looked at my calendar with fresh eyes, and saw how much of the busyness was self-inflicted. Within a week I killed 3 recurring meetings, and nobody missed them.

What burnout taught me: rest isn't a reward for finishing the work, because the work is never finished. If the business can't survive two weeks without you, that's a design flaw, not a badge of honor. And exhaustion is not a personality trait.

The sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need most.

When was your last real break?
L22:
This week we made hire number 50.

Three years ago we were 4 people in a garage in Denver. Folding tables, a space heater, a whiteboard bought off Craigslist. I keep scrolling through old photos of that garage and feeling more gratitude than I know what to do with.

Today we serve 900 customers. The growth is nice. What I'm actually proudest of is that the values we scribbled on that Craigslist whiteboard still run the company: customers first, default to transparency, hire people better than yourself.

To our first 4: thank you for believing when there was nothing to believe in. To our newest 46: thank you for choosing us. To our 900 customers: everything we build is for you.

Milestone noted. Back to work.
L23:
Networking events are mostly useless. I say that as someone who's been to every conference, every mixer, every founder happy hour, and collected hundreds of business cards along the way.

Clients from all of it: zero.

My last 3 clients came from writing online.

Writing wins on scale: a conversation reaches one person, a post reaches thousands. It wins on selection: the right people come to you already sold on how you think. And it compounds. A good post keeps working for months. A handshake is forgotten by Monday.

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Relationships still matter. The best ones just start when someone reads your ideas and thinks, "this person gets it."

Stop collecting business cards. Publish your thinking instead.
L24:
Forecast error down 18%. That's the result at one of our pilot customers, and the number I kept coming back to on episode 142 of Supply Chain Weekly, where we talked through AI demand forecasting.

An 18% cut in forecast error means less overstock, fewer stockouts, and working capital freed up. Nothing abstract about it.

On the episode we got into why traditional forecasting breaks down in volatile markets, what AI-driven forecasting looks like in practice once the buzzwords are stripped off, and the hard parts: data quality, change management, and why the forecasting team's expertise matters more with AI in the loop.

Thanks to the hosts for questions that went past the surface.

If you work in supply chain, operations, or planning, the episode is linked in the first comment.
L25:
Our year in review: ARR grew from $1.2M to $3.4M, the team grew from 9 to 21, and NPS sits at 61.

That NPS is the number I care most about, because growth means nothing if customers don't love what you build.

Now the mistake I'd take back: we hired sales too early. Reps came on board before we, the founders, had nailed the sales motion ourselves. What followed was months of missed targets and frustrated reps, and none of it was their fault. You can't hand off a playbook you haven't written. We eventually rebuilt the process from first principles and things clicked, but I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing the mistake because year-in-review posts tend to show only the highlight reel. Growth is messy.

Here's to the year ahead.
